figures.caption: Figure 4: (A) Krippendorff’s α (ties excluded) for evaluating inter-annotator agreement per judgment dimension. Dashed lines mark “tentative” (α = 0.67) and “good”(α = 0.80) agreement thresholds [18]. (B) ROC-AUC [4] for predicting pairwise human preference from automatic metric deltas, VLM annotations, and a logistic regression combining both metric deltas trained on a 50% subset of human annotations (Joint LR). Error bars indicate 95% CI over 10 random splits. Human annotations are reliable but noisier for temporal similarity. Our metrics show better alignment with human preferences than VLM-as-a-judge in their respective dimensions.

Figure 1: Animation2Code is the first benchmark to evaluate de-rendering of web animations to executable code. Animation2Code comprises 1,069 high-quality web animation videos (four examples shown, five uniformly sampled frames each from videos rendered at 30 FPS) paired with HTML/CSS/JavaScript code (right).

Table 2: Test set zero-shot, supervised finetuning, and iterative refinement performance across models and input settings. Best score under each metric is highlighted in bold. Exec% denotes the percentage of examples where the generated code executes successfully. While some models achieve nearperfect execution and strong appearance similarity, temporal similarity remains uniformly low across settings, highlighting a consistent gap in replicating animation dynamics.

Figure 7: Average appearance and temporal similarity across iterations over four method variants. Iterations stop at the best iteration. Dual Critic outperforms all other variants on both metrics, with all variants improving the most in the first iterations and plateauing as iterations increase.
Figure 5: Qualitative examples from zero-shot baseline models. All models struggle with precise motion and spatial relationships, even when overall appearance is partially correct.

Figure 2: Evaluation metrics for Animation2Code. We isolate animated regions via cropping, compute appearance similarity using DreamSim with DTW alignment, and measure temporal similarity via tracklet displacement correlation aggregated with a Chamfer-style matching.
Figure 8: Input FPS and modality sweep over baseline models on test set.
Table 6: Frame rate ablation for zero-shot baselines. ↑ = higher is better.
Figure 6: Baseline performance by animation category. Appearance varies with visual complexity, but temporal performance remains consistently low across categories.

Figure 3: Pairwise win rates from human preference annotations (ties excluded). Rows indicate the preferred model over columns. GPT-5.4 is the most preferred over all tested models. Models that excel in appearance do not consistently achieve better temporal alignment.
Table 4: Logistic regression coefficients predicting pairwise human preference from metric deltas. Significant predictors (p < 0.05) are in bold. ntest = 308 for all dimensions.
